reference: Cut or trace a triangle on paper and place it on a grid. Mark its starting corners. Slide the triangle gently to a new place without rotating the paper. Compare each original corner with its matching new corner. They should all have travelled the same distance in the same direction.

reference: Saying slide it over there is not enough to reproduce a translation. Give a direction and distance for the horizontal move, then for any vertical move. The instruction three right and two up tells a partner exactly how to move every point on our unit grid.

reference: Label the original triangle corners A, B and C. Their images are the matching corners after the translation. Keep the labels paired so that A is compared with its own image, rather than whichever new corner happens to be closest. Matching points give reliable evidence about the movement.

reference: Vertex A starts at one, one. Translate the shape three units right and two units up. Predict the new coordinates of A. Think about which coordinate changes at each stage. Keep the other corners hidden for a moment so one checked point leads the method.

reference: Three right changes one, one to four, one. Two up then gives four, three. The image of A is four, three. This coordinate calculation records the slide shown on the grid. It does not rotate the point around the origin or exchange the two coordinate positions.

reference: B begins at three, one and moves to six, three. C begins at one, three and moves to four, five. Each first coordinate increased by three, and each second coordinate increased by two. Join the image vertices in the same order to obtain the translated triangle.

reference: If A moves three right but B and C stay still, the triangle changes shape. That is not a translation of the whole triangle. Repair the model by applying the same instruction to every vertex. Then compare the side lengths and corner angles with those of the original triangle.

reference: An invariant is something that stays the same during a transformation. In a translation, side lengths, angles and orientation stay the same. Position changes. The triangle can point the same way in a new location, so pointing direction alone does not tell us where it has moved.

reference: The vertical changes differ, so the two point movements do not follow one translation. Every point must move by the same horizontal and vertical amounts. Correct the second movement to two up, then check any remaining vertices. Equal changes are stronger evidence than a rough visual resemblance.
